title: RBI Proposes Sweeping Overhaul of Foreign Investment Rules With New Control Test
excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has released draft rules to replace the 2019 foreign investment framework, introducing a 10% voting rights threshold to define foreign control and raising the gift remittance cap to $250,000.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • RBI's draft rules propose a 10% voting rights threshold for defining foreign control.
  • Gift remittance cap raised from $50,000 to $250,000, limited to near relatives.
  • New framework consolidates foreign investment regulations into a single code.
  • Public comments on the draft rules are open until August 31, 2026.
New Foreign Investment Framework
›Draft replaces 2019 NDI Rules with a unified code.
›10% voting rights threshold defines foreign control.
›Consolidates FDI, FPI, and overseas listings regulations.
›Public comments accepted until August 31, 2026.

The Reserve Bank of India on Tuesday released a comprehensive draft framework to overhaul foreign investment rules, proposing to replace the existing Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, with a unified, principle-based regulatory code. The move follows a directive in the Union Budget 2026-27 to review and modernize the regulatory architecture governing overseas fund flows into India.

The draft Foreign Exchange Management (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2026, consolidates provisions governing entry routes, sectoral caps, pricing and payment mechanisms for foreign direct investment, foreign portfolio investment and direct overseas listings into a single framework. The RBI has sought public comments until August 31, according to Business Standard.

What the New Rules Propose

The draft retains the core distinction between FDI and FPI. Investments of 10% or more in the equity of a company or limited liability partnership will continue to be classified as FDI, while holdings below that threshold remain FPI. Crucially, the draft also allows FPI to be reclassified as FDI once an investor's stake reaches 10%, subject to regulatory conditions, according to the Economic Times.

Eligible investee entities under the new framework include companies, LLPs, investment vehicles such as REITs, InvITs, alternative investment funds, venture capital funds, as well as mutual funds and exchange-traded funds that invest more than 50% in equity. Partnership firms and proprietary concerns are also included.

For pricing, listed entities and investment vehicles must comply with SEBI regulations, while unlisted entities must follow internationally accepted valuation methodologies certified by a chartered accountant, merchant banker or cost accountant. Rights issues are exempt from pricing guidelines.

> **"Rights issues are exempt from pricing guidelines.

"Rights issues are exempt from pricing guidelines."**

The 10% Control Threshold Draws Scrutiny

The most contentious provision introduces a formal numerical test for foreign control. Under the proposed framework, an Indian entity would be deemed foreign-controlled if a foreign investor holds 10% or more of voting rights, can appoint a majority of directors, or can influence management and policy decisions.

"The RBI has introduced a numerical benchmark that does not presently exist and could expand the circumstances in which a foreign investor is regarded as exercising control and attract higher compliances."

— Anuroop Omkar, Founding Partner, AK & Partners

The proposal drew immediate concern from legal experts, according to Reuters. Anjali Malhotra, a regulatory partner at Nangia Global, said the implications of this quantitative threshold require careful evaluation, particularly for investors holding limited minority rights that do not amount to effective control.

Moin Ladha, partner at Khaitan & Co, warned that if retained, the threshold could reshape how governance rights are structured across mergers, private-equity transactions and joint ventures. Suresh Swamy of Price Waterhouse & Co said it remained unclear whether a 10% holding alone, or combined with management rights, would trigger the control designation.

Gift Remittance Changes
›Gift remittance cap increased to $250,000.
›Previously, the cap was $50,000.
›Transfers restricted to near relatives only.

Gift Remittance Cap Raised, Restricted to Relatives

In a move directly relevant to the Indian diaspora, the draft raises the ceiling for repatriable gift transfers from $50,000 to $250,000, aligning it with the Liberalised Remittance Scheme limit. However, such transfers will now be restricted to near relatives only, according to the Times of India.

The draft also permits foreign investment through subscriptions, purchases, gifts, pledges, depository receipts and share swaps. Investment vehicles may issue units against equity of special purpose vehicles they propose to acquire.

Governance and Overseas Listing Guardrails

The proposed rules formally define foreign-controlled entities as resident companies, LLPs and investment vehicles owned or controlled by overseas investors, enabling better tracking of downstream foreign investment. The RBI retains operational oversight, reporting and payment mechanisms, while the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade continues to interpret foreign investment policy provisions.

On overseas listings, the draft bars companies from listing abroad if they, their promoters or directors are debarred from capital markets, classified as wilful defaulters, declared fugitive economic offenders, or under investigation under the Companies Act, the Economic Times reported.

What Comes Next

Implications of the 10% Control Threshold
›New threshold could increase compliance for minority investors.
›Concerns raised about governance rights in transactions.
›Legal experts call for careful evaluation of implications.

The proposed overhaul is part of India's broader push to attract foreign investment through lower compliance costs and tax cuts, even as capital outflows persist. A government-constituted committee undertook the detailed review in consultation with stakeholders before the draft was prepared.

For NRI investors and the diaspora, the rules could simplify investment pathways while introducing new compliance obligations — particularly around the control threshold. Market participants and investors have until August 31 to submit feedback before the rules are finalized.
